title: The Gathering

pages.text:
*From the Walk-Book of Highstep, Day 33. Weather: gold. Distance: three miles. Direction: forward. At last I can write it.*

The sand was soft and grey, and it stuck to Mo’s bare feet in thick, damp clumps that felt less like walking and more like wading through wet flour. The air tasted of salt and cold iron, a sharp sting in the back of the nose that had nothing to do with pine resin. Tor’s steps had changed. They were no longer the heavy, rolling thuds of the road. They were slow, deliberate, almost shy. The moss on her back swayed gently, as if she were trying not to wake the pines sleeping in her hair.

Highstep moved in a long, quiet line. The rope bridges swayed without a sound. Nobody laughed. Nobody complained about the bumps, because there were no bumps, only a steady, rhythmic rocking that felt like being held. Gran walked at the front, her staff tapping the sand with a precise *tick-tick-tick*. Mo pressed his heel into the ground, feeling the vibration travel up through his bones. It was not a step. It was a note, low and deep, humming in his teeth.

That night, the village did not sleep. They sat on the sand, wrapped in wool ponchos, watching the dark water lap against their toes. Mo stood on the Footpost, which they had carried down the Last Ladders and set in the mud. He felt the shiver. It was a chord so wide and so deep that the sand beneath his feet seemed to breathe.
pages.image: Mo, a small barefoot boy in a green poncho, stands on a flat stone on a grey sandy beach at dusk, eyes closed, feeling the vibration of a giant mossy mountain-creature resting nearby in the mist.

pages.text:
The mist pulled back like a curtain drawn by a giant hand, and the sea opened up, wide and silver-gold, stretching out to a horizon that looked like a drawn line. Then, out of the white haze, the others came.

Six mountains. They moved with the same slow, ancient grace, their legs the size of hills, their backs heavy with life. One was capped in snow, bright and silent. Another wore a coat of red autumn trees, rustling with the wind. A third had a lake on her back, clear and still, with tiny fishing boats moored to her horns. They were all different, all shaggy, all carrying their villages in their hair and on their shoulders.

The bells began to ring. Not all at once, but one after another, mountain to mountain, a sound that traveled across the water and settled in the chests of everyone on the shore. It was a greeting. It was a recognition. Mo looked at Tor, whose eyes were half-open, her small, kind gaze fixed on the others. She hummed. It was not a sound. It was a feeling, a deep, warm presence that filled the space between the mountains.
pages.image: Six colossal, moss-covered mountain-creatures emerge from white mist on a golden sea, each carrying a tiny village on its back, while Mo and Junie watch from the sandy shore in the foreground.

pages.text:
It was a festival that had no end and no beginning. Tents of bright wool and canvas popped up on the sand like mushrooms after rain. Banners snapped in the sea breeze, and long tables were set with bowls of soup, baskets of bread, and wheels of cheese that looked like gold coins. Pipes played a melody that went up and down the scale, and drums beat a steady, heavy rhythm that matched the pulse of the mountains.

Children who had never met before ran together, their faces smeared with sand and berry juice. They chased each other around the legs of the mountains, which were as wide as streets. Junie’s yellow scarf was knotted around her wrist, a ribbon from a stranger was in her hair, and her curls were wild and free. She was laughing, a sound that Mo had missed more than he could say.

Mrs. Cobb, stout and determined, held a single oyster on a silver plate. She looked at it. She looked at the other villagers. She took a bite, closed her eyes, and shook her head.

"Not for her," she declared, and put it back on the plate.

Highstep’s cheese, however, was a great success. It was gone before the sun was high.
pages.image: A vibrant beach festival with colorful tents and long tables; a stout woman in a straw hat holds a plate with an oyster, looking skeptical, while children run joyfully around the massive stone-grey legs of a mossy mountain.

pages.text:
Gran found him on a rock that looked like a broken molar, a very small, very old man with a beard that reached his knees. He was the Stepkeeper of the mountain with the red trees. His spectacles were so thin they looked like frost on a windowpane, and he held a book bound in leather so old it had worn soft as a favorite wool scarf.

They sat down. They did not speak. They opened their books.

Gran’s Walk-Book was thick, heavy as a sack of flour. The old man’s was thin, fragile, its pages soft as cloth. They read. They laughed at the same typos. They cried at the same storms. They traded a thousand years in an afternoon, passing pages back and forth like cards in a game.

Mo stood behind them, listening. He heard a fragment, a whisper in the paper, a line that was the same in every book, for every mountain, for every Stepkeeper who had ever held a pen.

"Weather: fair. Distance: none. Direction: home."
pages.image: Two tiny old figures, one a woman with a white braid and one a man with a long white beard, sit on a rock reading a large book together on a beach, with the massive legs of a mountain visible in the background.

pages.text:
The evening light turned the water into molten copper. The seven mountains gathered in a loose circle, their heads low, their horns touching the sky. Then, they sang.

It was not a song of words. It was a chord, a low, resonant vibration that rolled across the water and lifted every hair on every head. It was a farewell, and it was a welcome. It was the sound of roots letting go, and the sound of roots growing deep.

Mo stood on the Footpost, his bare feet pressed into the wet sand. He felt Tor’s answer through his heels. It was enormous. It was calm. It was a promise. He knew what came next. He did not fear it. He leaned forward, and for the first time, he did not need to listen with his feet. He listened with his whole self.
pages.image: Seven giant mossy mountain-creatures stand in a circle on a golden sea at sunset, their heads bowed, while a small barefoot boy in a green poncho stands on a stone in the foreground, eyes closed, feeling the vibration.
